content: The Global HIV Strategic Information Working Group Biobehavioural Survey Guidelines for Populations at Risk for HIV is a comprehensive document authored by a team of experts from various organizations, including the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), FHI 360, the Joint United Nations Programme on HIV/AIDS (UNAIDS), and the World Health Organization (WHO). The authors include Abu Abdul-Quader, Mark Berry, Trista Bingham, Janet Burnett, Maxia Dong, Amy Drake, Avi Hakim, Wolfgang Hladik, Angele Marandet, Anne McIntyre, Chris Murrill, Joyce Neal, and Nita Patel from the CDC, among others. The editors and reviewers also include a wide range of professionals from these and other institutions, ensuring the document's credibility and depth. The guidelines aim to address the global public health challenge posed by HIV by providing a standardized approach to conducting biobehavioural surveys (BBS). These surveys are essential tools for measuring the burden of HIV and associated risk factors, particularly among key populations at increased risk, such as men who have sex with men, sex workers, people who inject drugs, transgender individuals, and prisoners. These populations are often marginalized and difficult to reach through conventional survey methods, necessitating innovative and complex sampling designs. The document emphasizes the importance of accurate measurement in addressing public health problems. It provides detailed guidance on all aspects of survey implementation, from planning and design to data collection, analysis, and dissemination. The guidelines include updated methodologies, such as respondent-driven sampling, biomarker testing, and population size estimation, to ensure the collection of high-quality, actionable data. They also offer ready-to-use electronic questionnaires and a comprehensive appendix of indicators to standardize data collection and improve comparability across countries and over time. The guidelines are designed to be adaptable to various contexts and are intended to support public health workers, researchers, and policymakers in their efforts to improve HIV prevention, care, and treatment services. By standardizing survey methods and promoting the use of common indicators, the guidelines aim to enhance the quality and utility of survey data, enabling more effective public health programming and policy development. The document also highlights the importance of formative assessments to gather initial information about target populations, as well as the use of aggregate viral load metrics to monitor the prevalence of unsuppressed viral load at the population level. It underscores the need for collaboration among global, regional, national, and local actors to address gaps in access to HIV services and to track progress in the fight against the epidemic. The authors and contributors express their hope that these guidelines will serve as a valuable resource for anyone involved in conducting biobehavioural surveys, whether experienced or new to the field. By providing clear guidance and practical tools, the guidelines aim to strengthen the capacity of public health professionals to collect timely and reliable data, ultimately supporting strategic efforts to reduce the impact of HIV among key populations.
